newsitem.title: CHINA: Secure warehouses seen key to China metal finance.
newsitem.headline: Secure warehouses seen key to China metal finance.

text.p: Chinese base metal enterprises are in great need of financing for the stocks they hold and a network of secure warehouses is crucial, metal producers and bankers said at a conference here.
"The system for warehousing management is a very important link in the finance chain," a senior Chinese trader said.
Chinese metal producers concurred, saying they faced a cash crunch.

"We've had a capital shortage for a long time. Finance is really a problem, (stock financing) is an area where we can cooperate with foreign banks," the head of a major Chinese smelter told a conference on China's commodity and trade financing held in Shenzhen on Sunday and Monday.
Warehouses were necessary when, for example, a smelter could not sell metal if the price was too low, thus slashing earnings.
Instead of halting further production, the smelter could store unsold material in a secure warehouse and convince bankers to lend money against it, a senior industry official told the conference.
When traders requested financing, bankers usually first asked where the metal was, said the official, who asked that his name not be published.
"If the place is secure, geographically correct, at free disposal when needed with no legal or fiscal constraints, the deal can be made easier between the two parties," he said.
China's warehouses were not secure enough to satisfy bankers that metal stored in them would be retrievable as collateral should a borrower fail to repay loans, bankers said.
Bonded warehousing was vitally important for trade, brokers said.

"The main issue is whether the collateral is valued and viewed the same way as elsewhere. The financial security of the collateral, the metal and its exportability, are extremely important," the industry official said.

Traders and financiers liked to see cargo in a port, in a bonded location, a service offered by the London Metal Exchange (LME), with no movement restrictions in case of emergency, another industry official said.
"Local governments, where LME warehouses are located, have no influence on the movement or amount of stocks, free flow of tonnages in and out of the bonded warehouse is secured," he said.
Foreign bankers called on China to strengthen laws protecting their interest and told Reuters that in their dealings with China, they were frequently unsure about what practices were allowed.

One Western banker, active in commodity financing in China, related an incident where his bank took over merchandise in China offered as collateral, but was unable to get permission to export the material or sell it to other provinces.
Metals brokers said they still faced the touchy issue of whether to deal directly with enterprises or go through the centralised China National Import Export Corp (CNIEC).
"Enterprises now see the benefits of going directly to where the best deal is," one senior broker said.
